Article 1: Sending

161. The risen Christ, King of the Universe, sends His apostles to all nations to continue His own redeeming mission which “is to enable people to share in the communion that exists between the Father and the Son.”186 Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you (Mt 28:19-20).

162. This sending has two characteristics:

- A universal dimension: all men are called to be a part of the Kingdom of God, since God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4).

- The certainty of divine help: I am with you always, to the close of the age (Mt 28:20); they went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them... (Mk 16:20).

Article 2: Proclamation of the Kingdom

163. In virtue of this sending, the Church’s mission is the proclamation of the Kingdom of God. “The kingdom of God is not a concept, a doctrine, or a program subject to free interpretation, but it is before all else a person with the face and name of Jesus of Nazareth, the image of the invisible God.”187 The Church carries out this mission to liberate men from sin and death: When you were dead [in] transgressions... he brought you to life along with him, having forgiven us all our transgressions (Col 2:13). The principal promoter is the Holy Spirit, who acts in the Apostles and in the whole Church.188

164. That is why fidelity to the Holy Spirit permits us to overcome all the difficulties that the Church finds in her mission: prohibition against evangelization, obstacles from local cultures, lack of fervor, divisions among Christians, de-Christianization in countries of long-standing Christian tradition, a decrease in missionary vocations, a poor witness of the faithful, indifferent mentalities, and others.189 It is the Holy Spirit who guides us to the complete truth.190

Article 3: Witnessing

165. The Church’s mission is carried out by every Christian, and in a particular way, by those who have consecrated themselves to God in apostolate. Their purpose is identical to the Church’s purpose: to bring all men to conversion to God, to “a complete and sincere adherence to Christ and His Gospel through faith,”191 which must result in the worthy reception of the Sacraments.

166. In this apostolic work where “we are missionaries above all because of what we are... even before we become missionaries in word or deed,”192 our testimony of life – the “first and irreplaceable form of mission”193 – occupies the first place so that the charity of Christ may shine among the faithful.194

Article 4: Apostolic Commitments

169. The Institute of the Incarnate Word will take on the works of apostolate most conducive to the inculturization of the Gospel. For this reason, there are various Directories that complement the Constitutions. These Directories deal with apostolic action in the most urgent and important fields.

170. We list the preferred fields of apostolate here:

171. a) Spiritual dimension. The Institute will accomplish evangelization of the culture by sanctifying people individually. This will be done preferably by using the Spiritual Exercises according to the method and spirit of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and by spiritual direction.

172. b) Intellectual dimension. The Institute gives priority to: priestly formation in seminaries; education on all levels; the formation of lay leaders by means of courses in Catholic culture; the media.

Article 6: Educational Apostolate

178. Any religious dedicated to education will try to immerse themselves in an absolute and total love for the truth. Saint Thomas says, “We must consider that in any art the one who arranges the art and is called the architect is absolutely better than any manual laborer who carries out what is designed for him by another. But the bishops are like the principal artisans who command and arrange how the mentioned workers ought to conduct their duties, which is why they are called “episcopi,” i.e. superintendents. Therefore, it is absolutely better to teach theology and more meritorious if it is done with good intention, than to devote particular care to the salvation of this one and that... PART 7

FORMATION OF MEMBERS

105

CHAPTER 1 DIMENSIONS OF THE FORMATION

195. We want to form the members of our Institute in human and Christian maturity so that they reach the extent of the full stature of Christ (Eph 4:13).

With their works, members should demonstrate that they have God in their hearts because every tree is known by its own fruit (Lk 6:44), and faith, if it has no works, is dead (Jas 2:17).

We can organize this work into four sections: Human formation; Spiritual formation; Intellectual formation; Apostolic and pastoral formation. Nothing is better on this topic than the teachings of Blessed John Paul II,209 which we embrace as our own.

Article 1: Human Formation

196. Human formation is the basis of religious and priestly formation. Misunderstanding the relationship between nature and grace is the root of many evils. Grace does not destroy nature, but rather heals it, raises it, perfects it, dignifies it, and ennobles it. Nature is not only the foundation of grace, as though it were a mere external condition, but it belongs to the very essence of Christian identity and remains perfected. At the same time, grace transcends nature. Nature is subordinate to grace, as the obediential potency to its perfective act. Thus the natural has relative autonomy subordinate to the supernatural.

197. Because of the greater demands of his vocation, the priest should reflect – as should every Christian – the Incarnation of the

209 PDV 42-59.

107

Word, in whom human perfection and divine perfection shine, in intimate union but without blending together. Moreover, the priest, taken from among men and made their representative before God (Heb 5:1), must serve as a bridge, and not as an obstacle to others; he should make his ministry acceptable and believable from a human standpoint.

198. He “should be able to know the depths of the human heart, to perceive difficulties and problems, to make meetings and dialogue easy, to create trust and cooperation, to express serene and objective judgments.” Therefore, there is a need “for them to be balanced people, strong and free.”210

- Balanced: we must be priests who remain focused on the whole and not on just a single part, who don’t become overlyexcited with what they consider the whole; they must not let themselves be overcome by a depressive attitude that sees more evil than good, and must instead make room in their soul for all things, without despising or minimizing anything, but with hierarchy and order.

- Strong: we must be priests who do not allow ourselves to be carried away by every wind of doctrine and novelty, priests who move ourselves and judge by principles, who are neither softhearted and sentimental, nor hard and aloof.

- Free: we must be priests who do everything out of love, who do good even when no one is obliges them, or because the Superior is watching, nor on account of commendations or rewards. We must not be obsequious with the superiors, or try to obtain advantages. As priests, we should know how to implement fraternal correction, without caring about what others think of us, and understand with Saint Teresa of Jesus “the nothingness of the world and how it would soon come to an end.”211

210 PDV 43.

199. “They need to be educated to love the truth, to be loyal, to respect everyone, to have a sense of justice, to be true to their word, to be genuinely compassionate, to be men of integrity, and especially, to be balanced in judgment and behavior.”212 Education for the love of truth must be carried out via extensive intellectual formation, which is ordered to the truth and is unsatisfied with mere theological opinions. It must be a philosophical formation, as Saint Justin understood it. This formation will include theorizing, intellectual leisure, and sincere debate, which is a shared search for truth. Classes need to be moments in which true teaching and learning take place. “A simple and demanding program for this human formation can be found in the words of the apostle Paul to the Philippians: Whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is gracious, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things (Phil 4:8).”213

200. Along with intellectual formation, the will must be appropriately formed through constant practice of the virtues and control of passions, so that we are seeking and choosing only the greater good, always and everywhere. We want to form men who are authentically free and masters of themselves, who by that selfmastery are capable of giving themselves totally. We regard the practice of sports, camping, community vacations, etc., to be of great importance in this formation of the will.

Article 2: Spiritual Formation

201. The supernatural end of man corresponds to the natural end, but at the same time, transcends it: man’s desires are completely brought to rest in the beatific vision.214 During the time of formation, we must keep in mind this correspondence and transcendence. Pius XI teaches, “The Christian education encompasses the entire human life... to elevate, regulate, and perfect it according to the example and doctrine of Christ.”215

202. Spiritual life must be understood “as a relationship and communion with God.”216 “Spiritual training ...should be imparted in such a way that students might learn to live in an intimate and unceasing union with the Father through His Son Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit.”217 Therefore, spiritual life is a form of friendship: I no longer call you slaves, because a slave does not know what his mas-ter is doing. I have called you friends, because I have told you everything I have heard from my Father (Jn 15:15). This friendship has the characteristics of a true search:218 the priest must have an unquenchable thirst for God. He must never oppose “the search for the truth and the certainty of already knowing the fountain of this truth.”219 This search is possible because in some way we have already found the truth; however, we must make our relationship even more intimate. There is a threefold path to this encounter:220 meditation on the Word of God; participation in the Sacred Mysteries; fraternal charity, especially with those most in need.

203. - Faithful meditation on the Word of God is how we know the divine mysteries and make its values our own. This is particularly related to prophetic ministry.221 We take to heart the teaching of the Second Vatican Council: “All clerics, particularly priests of Christ and others who, as deacons or catechists, are officially engaged in the ministry of the Word, should immerse themselves in the Scriptures by constant sacred reading and diligent study. For it must not happen that anyone becomes an empty preacher of the Word of God to others, not being a hearer of the Word in his own heart.”222 The response to lectio divina is prayer, “which is without any doubt of primary value and a demand of spiritual formation...” because “the priest is the man of God, the one who belongs to God and makes people think about God.” Moreover, “one aspect of the priest’s mission, and certainly by no means a secondary aspect, is to become a ‘teacher of prayer’”; therefore, “the priest needs to be formed to have a deep intimacy with God.”223 The fruits of this intimacy with God and of the work of the Holy Spirit in the soul of the priest are discernment, relishing the presence of God, accepting His will, and rightly judging matters.224

Article 3: Intellectual Formation

219. The intellectual formation of future priests is an urgent issue facing the New Evangelization and the subject of modern challenges. This formation “is a fundamental demand of human intelligence by which one “participates in the light of God’s mind” and seeks to acquire a wisdom, which in turn opens to and is directed toward knowing and adhering to God.”244 This formation includes two phases, one ordered to the other: the study of philosophy, and the study of the Sacred Science.

220. “A crucial stage of intellectual formation is the study of philosophy, which leads to a deeper understanding and interpretation of the person, and of the person’s freedom and relationships with the world and with God.”245 This study is urgent, not only in view of later theological studies, but also in light of a particular cultural situation that exalts subjectivism as the criteria and measure of the truth.246 A “certainty of the truth” is necessary, and this is given only by a sound philosophy, founded in the objective reality of things, since “intelligence... is able to arrive at what is.”247 Without it, there is no basis for a total personal abandonment to Jesus and the Church since, “If you are not sure about the truth, how can we risk our own life and be strong enough to seriously question the life of others?”248 That is why the study of philosophy leads the future priest to lovingly embrace the truth, which in turn leads him to recognize that this truth is not created and measured by man, but granted to him as a gift by the Supreme Truth, God. Human reason, even with limitations and difficulties, can reach objective universal truth, even in reference to God and existence in its radical sense. He must learn that faith itself cannot do without reason or the effort to ponder over the contents of faith, as Saint Augustine attested: “I have wished to see with understanding what I have believed by faith, and I have debated and worked hard.”249

He is the light of the Paginae Sacrae: He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Lk 24:45). He is the center of the Sacred Scriptures as He, Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, ... interpreted to them what referred to him in all the scriptures (Lk 24:27). Thus, “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”250 Therefore, Sacred Scripture is the “soul” of theology.251

Article 1: Minor Seminary

Article 2: Postulancy

236. The period of postulancy is a time of first contacts with the members of the Institute, with the purpose of familiarizing the candidate with the charism of the order and with the obligations of the novitiate. This contact will be carried out by one or several priests, as designated by the Provincial Superior, who must know the candidate, his vocation and his suitability, in order to present him to the novitiate.

237. The duration of the postulancy is not fixed but depends on the candidate’s preparation, his level of Christian and human maturity, his basic general culture, his emotional balance, and his capacity to live in community, etc.,282 because “most of the difficulties found nowadays in the formation of novices come from the fact that they don’t have the minimum necessary maturity when admitted to the novitiate.”283 So that “nobody will be admitted without adequate preparation,”284 this period is required. Postulancy will not last more than two years.

The novitiate lasts for one year. “The novitiate, through which life in an institute is begun, is arranged so that the novices better understand their divine vocation, and indeed one which is proper to the institute; so that they experience the Institute’s way of life, and form their mind and heart in its spirit; and so that their intention and suitability are tested.”285

Article 4: Profession

a. Temporary Profession

251. In order to be valid, temporary profession requires:

1. that the person making it is at least eighteen years of age;

2. that the novitiate has been made validly;

3. that the profession be explicit and made without force, fear, or deceit;

4. that the profession be received by the Provincial Superior, personally or through another.

252. Upon completion of the novitiate, a novice will be admitted to temporary profession. The admission is decided by the Provincial Superior with the deliberative vote of the Council. When there are doubts concerning the vocation, either from the candidate or the Institute, the time of novitiate may be prolonged, but not for longer than a period of six months.290

Article 5: Religious Seminary

a. Seminary for Religious Who Are Candidates to the Priesthood

258. The Institute of the Incarnate Word is a clerical institute, wherein the majority of the members are priests. Upon finishing the novitiate, a new period of priestly formation begins, executed according to Canon Law for the formation of clerics and according to the documents of the Holy See, and always in accordance with the spirituality and mission of the Institute, so as to accomplish an authentic overall formation: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

134

259. According to our own charism, we strive to orient all our studies toward the evangelization of the culture, for which we will spare no efforts or means. We are not content with a merely superficial knowledge of philosophy and theology that is incapable of understanding the modern exercise of atheism in all its depth, and is thus incapable of providing a remedy for it.

b. Seminary of the Coadjutor Brothers

260. The Institute will also have religious called “coadjutor brothers.” They will dedicate themselves to serving the houses and to giving spiritual services that do not require the sacramental grace of Holy Orders.

261. These brothers should complete formation in the seminary, where they will take some courses in philosophy and theology, “attending to the needs of the Church and the circumstances of men and the times, according to the end and the character of the Institute.”292 The coadjutor brothers will continue their formation, under the direct authority of the local superior, until their perpetual profession in the houses to which they are assigned. Their ongoing formation must be monitored.

Article 6: Ongoing Formation

262. Religious life is a process of continual conversion that does not end with the years of formation, but must be maintained and must grow every day.293 Regarding our pastoral work, this formation is an act of true and proper justice for God’s people, who always demand the most appropriate answer from us.294

292 Cf. CIC, c. 659 § 1-2.

135

263. Ongoing formation, not limited by the age or circumstances of the member, possesses four dimensions: human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral.

264. We believe that permanent and ongoing formation is fundamental. To accomplish this, in addition to ordinary measures such as conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc., extraordinary measures should be taken whenever possible, for example: the 30day spiritual exercises every ten years, pilgrimages to the Holy Land and to great shrines of Christianity, etc.

265. In order to undertake this ongoing formation, we desire that all the members of our Institute take ecclesiastical or civil courses after the Seminary, according to their capacities and talents. These will be taken preferably in the pontifical universities of Rome or in those institutions recognized by the Holy See, so as to receive the qualifying degree of licentiate and doctorate.295 We already have a priestly community in Rome where two years are normally spent for this purpose.296 The formation in Rome implies the attainment of a Roman spirit, which entails a “crown of virtues: universal openness, fidelity to the Magisterium, a missionary spirit, endurance, and magnanimity.”297 Being in Rome is a “situation that permits [one] to live the supernatural reality of communion with the Church of Rome and with the Bishop of Rome. In the ecclesiastical experience [one] enters into the field of a new reality: [one] experiences the communion with all who are in communion with the Church of Rome.”298 Therefore, the opportunity to study in the Eternal City has a two-fold advantage: “It means having the advantage of living in a community either of priests or seminarians, and having access to the scholarship available in or through the Roman universities. It means being witnesses, day after day, to the living tradition of the faith as it is proclaimed in the See of Peter.”299

Article 7: Those Responsible for the Formation

268. We will take special care preparing and choosing those priests in charge of the formation of seminarians, as the future of the Institute depends on it. This is what we mean by “to form a school”: that those priests in charge of the formation of our future priests must be able to transmit the heritage of our Institute, as opposed to forming a “solitary” priest, that is, one who would not contribute to the continuation of our work. In the work of evangelizing the culture, the efforts of one individual or one generation are not sufficient; rather, a great evangelical movement is necessary, one that will forever deepen and extend itself in this task. This is the work of those responsible for formation. Therefore, those in charge of formation must be formed themselves as men of suitable discernment who are rich in spirit.

269. Besides sufficient knowledge of Catholic doctrine regarding faith and morals, the task of forming others demands certain conditions. These conditions are: human intuition and warmth, familiarity with God and prayer, wisdom, love for liturgy, necessary cultural competence, availability, and willingness to dedicate personal care to each of the seminarians individually, and not merely to the group. PART 8

GOVERNMENT OF THE INSTITUTE

Introduction: The Religious Family of the Incarnate Word

271. The Institute of the Incarnate Word recognizes the primary and supreme authority of the Supreme Pontiff, and professes not only obedience to him, but also fidelity, filial submission, adherence, and disposition for the service of the universal Church.

272. Ever docile to the will of God, superiors will regard the exercise of their authority as true service to the Church and will always remember that the primary obligation of the superior is to command well.

Article 1: Female Branch: The Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará

273. Both “the Institute of the Incarnate Word” and its female branch, “the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará” form the “Religious Family of the Incarnate Word.” Both Institutes are indissolubly united. Their union is spiritual, though legally independent. Their spiritual union is given essentially through possessing the same founder and twin Constitutions, by the Spiritual Father (elected by the women religious), and by the help of other priests of the Institute of the Incarnate Word (spiritual advisers, community advisers, spiritual directors, confessors, professors, etc.) who are appointed for these tasks by the competent authority.

Article 2: Contemplative Branch

274. The male contemplative branch is also part of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. It is comprised of those houses where the religious dedicate themselves to the contemplative life in conformity with the provisions of proper law.

275. Every monastery should have a superior designated by the Superior General with the consent of his council.

276. The monasteries are houses of the Institute belonging to the province in whose territory they are located.

Article 3: Third Order

277. The Institute of the Incarnate Word also has a Third Order. Third Order “members live in the world but share in the spirit of ... [the] institute, under... [its] overall direction...”305

278. The Third Order is structured on three levels, according to the degree of commitment which the members freely choose:

- First Degree: Lay associates who aspire to evangelical perfection according to the spirit of the Institute by participating in its mission,306 obligating themselves freely through private vows or some other sacred bond.

305 Cf. CIC, c. 303.

306 Cf. CIC, c. 725.

- Second Degree: Lay associations of the faithful: groups or movements, each with its own structure, that want to participate in the spirit and purpose of the Institute.

- Third Degree: All faithful lay people related in different ways to the Institute, who want to share in its spirit: friends, acquaintances, benefactors, family members, etc.

279. The Third Order is united to and dependent upon our Religious Family in both aspects, in groups and individually.

280. The Superior General, with the deliberative vote of his Council, chooses the Major Adviser, the liaison between the Institute and the Third Order. Each Provincial Superior, in conjunction with the Provincial Superior of the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará, is the liaison in his province, and gives spiritual assistance to the tertiaries, according to the three levels of the Third Order.

Article 4: Central Coordinating Board

281. The Superior General of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, or his delegate, will preside over the Central Coordinating Board, made up of: the Superior Generals of both Institutes; the superiors of each Institute, Movement, and Association of the Third Order. CHAPTER 3 GENERAL GOVERNMENT

Article 1: Superior General

295. The Institute is permanently governed by a Superior General assisted by his Council of five Councilors. Of the six members of the General Government, the Superior General and at least two Councilors will be elected by the Chapter. The Vicar General, the General Secretary, and the General Treasurer are named by the Superior General.

296. The Superior General holds the highest rank in the Institute and exercises the functions of primary authority. He attends to the care and government of the Institute of the Incarnate Word and of all its members according to the present Constitutions and Canon Law.

The Superior General’s jurisdiction of authority is over the entire Institute of the Incarnate Word and over each of its members, both in the apostolic and contemplative houses.

To be elected and to perform this office, he must possess ability, discretion, prudence, maturity, and the other virtues required for the sound performance of his duty.

To be elected, the Superior General must be a priest with at least fifteen years of perpetual profession318 in the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

He is elected for a period of six years and can be reelected.

318 Cf. CIC, c. 623.

155

297. - The voters must be careful not to elect anyone who has desired or sought the office of Superior General. The same applies for choosing the other superiors.

298. - The Superior General must avoid preferential treatment of members of the Institute. He must have the same attitude toward everyone, and avoid showing partiality. Preference of persons is a sin that opposes distributive justice – the principle of giving positions, offices, and responsibilities for the common good in proportion to the dignity or ability of each person. In justice, the person who is most suitable for each assignment must be chosen for the common good. Therefore, the person’s qualifications regarding his suitability must be considered. When we fail to do so, we commit the vice of partiality of persons. The person chosen in such a case is appointed because of who he is, and not because of his abilities; he therefore prevents the one who, in justice, should fill that office from doing so. This kind of injustice is expressly prohibited in Sacred Scripture.319 The Superior should be a father in the image of the Heavenly Father, Who shows no par-tiality (Acts 10:34).

299. - The Superior General is expected to be faithful to the Constitutions. He should not grant himself the authority to exempt anyone from honoring them even for minor reasons.

300. - He is never to reprimand in anger. He is to be gentle with all and strict with himself. He is never to speak in praise of himself except with the hope of bringing about some good, and even then only with humility and acknowledgment of God’s gifts.

301. - All functions and obligations flowing from his office as Superior General must be performed with a spirit of exceptional service. His authority is for service and his service is authoritative. He is to govern as one who serves, because he is obligated by reason of his office to serve by leading: Let the greatest among you be as the youngest, and the leader as the servant (Lk 22:26).

319 Cf. Dt 1:17; 16:19; Jas 2:9.

156

302. Faculties and duties of the Superior General are:

1st To govern the members as sons of God. The Superior General is to extend to them the same paternal charity that God has for them. He is also to have that fraternal charity desired by God in loving the other superiors and members. God also desires that they too love each other with the same fraternal charity.

2nd To respect each human person because of his dignity as a person, and even more so because of the added dignity flowing from baptism and consecration. Moreover, he is to respect them because of the combination of inborn and acquired abilities which make up the uniqueness of each member.

3rd To promote voluntary obedience, to foster willingness in obedience and submissive freedom. Whoever has freely professed obedience must voluntarily practice the specific acts of that counsel. The perfect attainment of this ideal will be the supernatural and human sign of the proper exercise of authority.

4th To listen willingly. To listen is neither to assent, nor to hear with deaf ears; neither is it the attention of a disciple, nor the instruction of a teacher. Listening does not require giving an answer, for indeed, an answer may not exist. Nor may it be prudent or obligatory to give any answer. Nor is it his duty to reach an agreement on what he and any member may have been talking about, as this agreement is often non-existent or impossible to attain. Nor is it his duty to make a decision that accommodates the desires of a member.

5th To foster his initiatives for the good of the Institute and the Church, because he is obligated to do so by his office, he must energetically resist any passivity, as if merely waiting for others to suggest initiatives.

157

6th To decide and to order what should be done, taking into account the executive power given by Canon law.320

303. The specific and proper functions of the Superior General, besides the ones already established by can. 619 of CIC, are the following:

1st To work for the preservation and growth of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

2nd To promote members’ knowledge and observance of the Holy See’s decrees relating to religious.

3rd To oversee observance of the Constitutions and fidelity to the spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word.

4th To promote as much as possible the spiritual and temporal good of all the members of the Institute, and to ensure that everyone fulfills his respective duties and obligations.

5th To preside over the sessions of the General Council and present therein all the matters to be addressed. The Superior General can seek advice from the Council any time he deems it necessary.

6th To notify the Provincial Superiors, and when he deems it appropriate, to directly notify the Local Superiors, of the Council’s resolutions that they should be aware of.

7th To visit all of the Provinces and houses of the Institute for inspection and general direction.

320 Cf. CIC, c. 137 and concordant paragraphs.

158

8th To oversee all aspects of the spiritual and intellectual formation of religious.

9th To convoke ordinary and extraordinary General Chapters, according to these Constitutions.

10th To grant the license to publish writings related to religious or moral matters.321

11th Within the limits of his proper competence, the Superior General can grant dispensations, that is, relaxations of merely ecclesiastical laws in a particular case,322 in every place, with respect to the members, and with respect to himself,323 according to the conditions demanded by Canon law.324

304. The Superior General also possesses other duties which he must execute together with his Council as determined in Chapter 4 (The Office of the General Chapter).

305. The Superior General can be removed from his office for the reasons stated in the Code of Canon law.325

CHAPTER 5 THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT

Article 1: Provinces

332. To make governance of the Institute easier and more effective, territorial divisions called provinces are permanently established, according to the various conditions of people, places and time.

333. The General Chapter, and the Superior General ad referen-dum of the General Chapter, are responsible for the establishment or modification of province and vice-province boundaries, in accordance with established norms. The following norms must be considered:

a) In order for a territory or a group of houses to constitute a province, at least three canonically established houses of the Institute of the Incarnate Word are required.

334. Under the direction of the Superior General and his Council, each province is governed by a Provincial Superior, assisted by four provincial Councilors.

Article 2: Provincial Superior

335. The priest appointed Provincial Superior must have the necessary physical and moral aptitude to execute the demands of this office, and must have at least 10 years of perpetual vows in the Institute. The General Superior, with the consent of his Council, can dispense with this condition.

10th To admit candidates to perpetual profession with the consent of the provincial council.

11th To exclude members from subsequent profession, after consulting his Council.344

12th To grant permission for a prolonged absence from the community.345

13th To grant permission in particular cases regarding the individual goods of those who are professing according to what is established in n. 70 of these Constitutions.346

CHAPTER 1 THE MYSTERY OF THE WORD

Introduction

1. We want to be anchored in the sacrosanct mystery of the Incarnation which is “the first and fundamental mystery of Jesus Christ.”1 Rooted in this mystery that is truly present among us, we want to fervently set out to restore all things in Christ (Eph 1:10). 3. We always want to draw new light and strength from the redeeming Incarnation, since Jesus Christ is the inexhaustible source of Being, Truth, Kindness, Beauty, Life and Love.

Article 1: Primacy of Jesus Christ

4. We profess the preeminence of Christ, even as a man, over all creation. He has primacy over the souls and bodies of the members of His mystical Body, and also over all men through all ages. He is the Head of everyone – even of those not predestined to eternal life in heaven with Him, who will only stop being potential members of the Body of Christ when they leave this world. The Son is “the Father’s work of art.”4

5. We profess that Christ is Head of the Church5 and of all men,6 and that He has triple primacy over them: a primacy of order, of perfection and of power. He has primacy of order because due to His closeness with God, His grace is the highest and the first – though not chronologically speaking. All who receive grace receive it in reference to His: For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29). He has primacy of perfection because He possesses the fullness of grace: We have beheld his glory... full of grace and truth (Jn 1:14). He has primacy of power because He has all the power to communicate grace and glory to all the members of His Body: And from his fullness have we all received, grace upon grace (Jn 1:16).

6. Therefore, heresies throughout the ages have had and will have a common denominator: to diminish the dignity of Jesus Christ. Saint Leo the Great pointed out: “We are assured that hardly anyone (any heretic) has gone astray except if he has failed to believe the reality of Christ’s two natures, and to acknowledge one Person at the same time.”7 Saint Thomas teaches that, “When one considers the errors of heretics, it is apparent that their main

Article 2: Love for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit

7. Contemplation on the mystery of the Incarnation nurtures love for the Holy Trinity – Father, Son and Holy Spirit – who was the actual author of the Incarnation. This contemplation also ignites in us an ardent love for the Word who “for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven.”11 It also nourishes love for the Word in His preexistence, His entering the world, His earthly life (works and teachings), His leaving the world, His mystical life and His second coming.

Article 3: Preexistence of the Word

8. a. Eternal Person. The person of the Word exists from all eternity: In the beginning was the Word... and the Word was God (Jn 1:1). We have to be convinced that “God loves Christ... more than He loves the entire created universe,”14 and, as Saint Teresa says, “God alone suffices.”15 In everything and for everything, we want to give primacy to the spiritual, and to surrender in holy abandonment to God’s “will of good-pleasure,” since as a response to the revelation of God, “man freely commits his entire self to God.”16

CHAPTER 2 THE MYSTERY OF THE INCARNATE WORD

Article 1: His First Coming

11. And the Word became flesh (Jn 1:14). The work of the Incarnation is shared among the three divine persons, but it is attributed to the Holy Spirit because: a) The supreme love of God is the cause of the Incarnation: For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (Jn 3:16). b) Human nature was not assumed by our own merit, but only by grace, which is attributed to the Holy Spirit: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit (1 Cor 12:4). c) Jesus Christ alone is holy and the only Son of God: The child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God (Lk 1:35); and because in Him we are made children of God: Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Gal 4:6); in Him we are sanctified, since He is the Spirit of holiness (Rom 1:4).

12. Based on the mystery of the Incarnation – the work of the Spirit in the Virgin Mary – we must always sing the mercies of God21 because “the immortality of blessedness becomes credible from the Incarnation of the Son of God.”22 We must understand clearly that without Jesus Christ, we can do nothing,23 and that we must always be inclined to grow in virtue with all our strength.

13. Therefore, we must be moved by the Holy Spirit and have utter docility to Him. To obtain this we need:

14. a) Attention to the Holy Spirit’s inspirations like the Virgin, who was worthy to be visited by the Angel Gabriel24 and to listen to him because of her habitual attentiveness to the motions of the Spirit. 15. b) Discernment of spirits in order to accept and follow the motions of the Holy Spirit, and to reject those of the evil spirit. We must be very prudent, in imitation of the Virgin who considered in her mind what sort of greeting this might be (Lk 1:29).

The Mother of God’s consent shows us that she was not “a mere passive instrument, but instead, she freely cooperated with the work of human salvation through faith and obedience.”27 Likewise, neither should we be passive instruments.

25 SAINT AMBROSE, Commentary on Saint Luke, 2, 19.

26 Cf. SAINT IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA, Spiritual Exercises, 322.

27 Cf. LG 56.

204

19. The Virgin gave her “yes” as a servant: I am the handmaid of the Lord (Lk 1:38), He has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid (Lk 1:48), and then the Word took the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7) in her pure womb. Therefore, our spirituality needs to be marked in a special way by professing a fourth vow of Marian slavery according to the spirit of Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort, so as to “marianize” our whole life. When we reach the chapter that speaks about vows, we will discuss our Marian spirituality further.

a. The Divinity of Jesus

20. Saint Peter’s confession has always been central to the Catholic faith: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Mt 16:16). This confession must be central to our spirituality, too. As taught by the successor of Peter, Blessed John Paul II, “We are only redeemed if Jesus Christ can in his own person fully communicate the divine life.”28 On another occasion, Blessed Pope John Paul II said that when professing Jesus is Lord (Rom 10:9),29 “We break with everything that claims to set itself up as an absolute, and we destroy the idols of money, power, sex, and those [idols] that are hidden in ideologies, ‘lay religions’ with totalitarian ambitions.”30

21. He is the “Way” to the Father, and nobody goes to the Father except through Him.31 His is the only name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). He is the one that makes the Church a “sacrament – a sign and instrument, that is, of communion with God and of unity among all men.”32 He alone sustains all the Church’s dogmas since He is “the truth that contains all the others.”33 He alone reveals to us the primacy and weight of eternity above all temporal reality.

28 BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the International Theological Commission, October 6, 1981; OR (10/25/1981) Spanish Edition.

29 Cf. 1 Cor 12:3; Jn 20:28.

30 BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the Latin-American Episcopal Conference, July 7, 1980; OR (7/13/1980) Spanish Edition.

31 Cf. Jn 14:6.

32 LG 1.

205

22. In addition, professing the divinity of Jesus Christ must move us to practice the virtues of transcendence: faith, hope and charity; and from practicing these, to the urgency of prayer and incessant contemplation, and to becoming conscious of the need to actively and passively purify the senses and the spirit.

23. In contemplating that the Incarnate Word is “God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father,”34 we want to put aside all attitudes of mere humanism (humanism without transcendence) that eventually annihilates man. We want to put aside all attitudes of false kenosis (emptying of oneself) that, based on an excuse of turning to that which is inferior, wind up emptying what is superior. “To be in the world” means that a person embraces the spirit of the world by emptying oneself and forgetting that Christians are in the world but not of the world (Jn 17:16). By “falling away from God altogether, [man] would cease to exist. For the glory of God is man fully alive; and man’s life consists of beholding God.”35

b. The Humanity of Jesus

24. Saint John the Baptist foretold Jesus: After me comes a man (Jn 1:30); Saint Peter denied Jesus before the servant girl: I do not know the man (Mt 26:72); and Pilate presented Him to the crowd: Ecce homo (Behold the man) (Jn 19:5). We profess that Jesus is not only God, but also true man, as the centurion did: Truly this man was the Son of God (Mk 15:39).

33 BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Address to the Pontifical Antonianum University, January 16, 1982; OR (1/31/1982) Spanish Edition.

34 COUNCIL OF NICEA I, The Nicene Creed.

35 SAINT IRENAEUS, Against the Heresies, 4, 20, 7.

206

25. Becoming man is “the first and fundamental mystery of Jesus Christ.”36 “God had never been so close to man – and never had man been so close to God – as in that very moment: in the instant of the Incarnation mystery!”37

26. The Word that not only expresses the Father, but also expresses the being and the work of all creatures,38 and in particularly of all men, male or female, “manifests man fully, and man discovers himself in the sublimity of his vocation,” in such a way that “it is only in the mystery of the Incarnate Word that the mystery of man truly becomes clear.”39

27. Derived from this, as from its root, is one of the main elements of our spirituality. As Terence said: “I am a man, and nothing human is alien to me.”40 Even more so, due to the Incarnation, nothing genuinely human is alien to us. Therefore, we must work to extend the Incarnation to all reality, specifically evangelizing the culture, because: “No human activity is foreign to the Gospel.”41

28. For us Christ is mysteriously identified with each man. Each and every man can be comprehended only in Jesus Christ: “It was necessary for mankind that God became man in order to demonstrate the dignity of human nature to mankind.”42 On judgment day He will say: For I was hungry and you gave me food... (Mt

36 BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, September 6, 1981; OR (9/13/1981) Spanish Edition.

37 BLESSED JOHN PAUL II, Angelus Message, August 2, 1981; OR (8/9/1981) Spanish Edition.

38 Cf. SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, ST I, 34, 3; I-II, 93, 1, ad 2: “And among other things expressed by this Word, the eternal law itself is expressed thereby.”

39 GS 22.

40 “Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto” He auton timoroumenos, v. 77 (Translation is ours).

42 SAINT THOMAS AQUINAS, Opuscula Theologica, Compendium of Theology, 381.

207

25:35). The poor are Christ: “They represent the role of the Son of God.”43 The pilgrims are Christ: “Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ.”44 The children are Christ: Whoever receives one child such as this in my name receives me (Mt 18:5). In every man, “Jesus is hidden in the depths of his soul.”45 Saint Augustine said: “In Him we are Christs and Christ.”46

29. All Christians, truly, should live a life in imitation of the Incarnate God. This truth is even greater for us, the religious of the family of the Incarnate Word. Not only are we to live Christ’s life looking for God in everything, but we are to spread that life to others, and to endow the cultures of man with Christ’s life in order to elevate him: “By his ignorance of the worthiness of his [own] nature, man is misled into clinging to things less than God in nature as to an end.”47

30. This mysterious and joyful reality of being “other Christs” (central to our spirituality) makes Saint Paul devise the words to express it: conmortui (2 Tm 2:11), consepulti (Rom 6:14), conresuscitati (Eph 2:6), convivificati (Eph 2:5), complantati (Rom 6:5), convivemus (2 Tm 2:11), consedere (Eph 2:6). This brings him to exclaim: It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20). Also, Blessed Elizabeth of the Trinity said so very beautifully that we should be “like a new incarnation of the Word,” “like another humanity of Christ,” so that the Father may only see “his beloved Son”48 in us.

31. In principle, we are already Christ by Baptism, but our task is to be Christ in the fullest sense, dying and living, as Saint Paul says: You also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in

43 SAINT VINCENT DE PAUL, Letters, 11, 32; ES XI, 725.

44 SAINT BENEDICT, Holy Rule, 53, 1.

45 SAINT THÉRÈSE OF LISIEUX, Story of a Soul, 9.

46 SAINT AUGUSTINE, Exposition on the Book of Psalms, 26, 2, 2. CCL 38,154 ff.

47 CG IV, 54.

48 BLESSED ELIZABETH OF THE TRINITY, Elevation 33. 34. 36.

208

Christ Jesus (Rom 6:11), and as Saint Peter says: He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live in righteousness (1 Pt 2:24).

32. Dying:

- to sin and to the works of the flesh since in Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace (Eph 1:7); those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires (Gal 5:24);

- to the pain of sin, that is to say, to the evil world: I have overcome the world (Jn 16:33), because before we were enslaved to the elemental powers of the world (Gal 4:3); and to hell because at the name of Jesus, every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth (Phil 2:10);

- to the fear of death since the Son of God has become flesh to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong bondage (Heb 2:15);

- to the power of the devil for the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (1 Jn 3:8);

- to the slavery of the old law: He redeemed us from the curse of the law (Gal 3:13).

33. Living:

- the life of grace in its fullness since Christ has come in flesh to bring us life and life in abundance.49 This life is the grace of God that makes us partakers of the divine nature (2 Pt 1:4). It is the supernatural life of the theological virtues, of the instilled moral virtues, and of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

49 Cf. Jn 10:10.

209

- the prophetic life by which we participate in “Christ’s prophetic office,”50 giving testimony of faith and charity, offering a sacrifice of praise to God, proclaiming the Word whether convenient or inconvenient,51 in preaching, teaching, writing, doing research, in evangelization, in catechesis, etc.

- the priestly life – both the common priesthood derived from baptism, and the ministerial or hierarchical priesthood (different from the common priesthood by essence, and not [merely] by degree).52

34. - In addition, we have to live the life of mastery over oneself.

a) A life of mastery includes dominion over oneself: in the measure that man triumphs over sin, he dominates the incentives of the flesh, and governs his soul and body. The religious, in the measure that he subjects his soul completely to God, becomes indifferent and detached from the things of the world. This doesn’t imply a powerlessness, but on the contrary, a dominant and free will, able to be devoted to things of the world without being dominated by them.

35. b) A life of mastery includes dominion over people: in the measure that the religious generously surrenders to the service of Jesus Christ – the only King that deserves to be served – he acquires an effective, though spiritual, royalty over men, even over those who have power and authority, and even over those who abuse it. This dominion comes about because the religious takes the burden of their sin and their hardships upon himself, by a humble and helpful love that comes through his self-sacrifice.

50 LG 12.

51 Cf. 2 Tm 4:2.

52 Cf. PIUS XII, Mediator Dei, 26-27; PO 2.

210

36. c) A life of mastery also includes dominion over the world:

- By collaborating with the created world through work, and with the redeemed world through apostolate. For this royalty to be effective, there must be a dedication to things, along with a detachment from and an indifference to these same things: From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the form of this world is passing away (1 Cor 7:29-31).

- By leaving the world behind, be it for fidelity to the same world (a means and not an end), or by fidelity to God, resisting concupiscence, temptations, and sins of the world; by being indifferent to the maxims, jeers and persecutions of the world, depending only on our good conscience illuminated by faith, ready for martyrdom – the full and total rejection of the evil world – for fidelity to God.

37. The highest grace that God can grant our young Religious Family is persecution53, especially that persecution that leads to martyrdom. “Jesus Christ always lives in order to give us the strength to support all hardships for His love. The works of God are always under attack so that the Divine Magnificence may shine forth.”54 We must always remember that for persecution to be blessed, it must fulfill two indispensable requirements: first, that we may be “persecuted for the sake of Christ,” and second, that what is said against us is false.55 We must be very careful not to return to our burdens, nor to spend time taking pleasure in them, nor to succumb to the “self-complacency of Lucifer which makes you imagine you are somebody,”56 and that we are suffering a great deal. “[Our] pride and sensitiveness make [us] magnify splinters into planks, scratches into wounds, molehills into mountains.”57

53 Letter to Diognetus, 5: “They love all men, and are persecuted by all... those who hate them are unable to assign any reason for their hatred.”

54 SAINT PAUL OF THE CROSS, Letter 47.

55 Cf. SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, Homilies on Saint Matthew, 15, 5.

211

38. d) Dominion over the devil: we need religious who are not only convinced that by the grace of God they have the power to resist the devil, but also are able to exorcise the devil.

39. We should live as if we were resurrected: Seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth (Col 3:1-2); we should live in the freedom of the children of God who are not enslaved:

* neither under the elemental spirits of the universe (Gal 4:3); * nor under the letter that brings death;58 * nor under the spirit of the world;59

because we must not submit again to the yoke of slavery... (otherwise) Christ would be of no benefit to us.60

40. We must be so docile to the Spirit that we could say, “My glory is to live as free as a bird in the sky; I don’t make a nest on this earth”; not owing anything to the flesh for all flesh is like grass and all its glory, like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls (1 Pt 1:24) and if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit (Gal 5:25), since what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit (Jn 3:6).

56 SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNION DE MONFORT, Letter to the Friends of the Cross, 48.

57 SAINT LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNION DE MONFORT, Letter to the Friends of the Cross, 48.

58 Cf. 2 Cor 3:6.

59 Cf. 1 Cor 2:12.

60 Cf. Gal 5:1-2.

212

41. This is akin to having the spirit of a prince,61 to guide the soul to great acts, to be concerned about the big things, to carry out great works with absolute virtue. This is to be noble. And what does it mean to be noble? It is a feeling, not a saying. It is a man with heart, a man that has something to give to himself and to others, a man born to lead. Nobles are able to punish themselves and others. They create a style by their conduct. They do not demand freedom but hierarchy. They set laws and fulfill them... They feel honor as life [itself]. They can give themselves because they possess themselves. They know at every instant what one must die for. They are able to give things that no one demands and abstain from things that no one prohibits. They always regard themselves as beginners. Let us always regard ourselves as beginners and seek always and unceasingly to aspire to a holier and more perfect life.

42. Thus, we firmly resolve to reach sanctity. A religious who is not willing to go through the second and third conversions, or who does nothing concrete to achieve them, does not actually belong to our spiritual family, though he may be with us in body. We must have “a great and very resolute determination to persevere until reaching the end, come what may, happen what may, whatever work is involved, whatever criticism arises, whether they [we] arrive or whether they die on the road, or even if they do not have courage for the trials along the way, or if the whole world collapses....”62 What matters is to take a step, one more step. It is the same step that always begins again.

43. Through baptism, the practice of virtues and religious profession, “deeply rooted in baptismal consecration and a fuller expression of it”,63 we seek to more closely imitate and perpetually represent in the Church of the way of life that the Son of God made His own when He became flesh.64

61 Cf. Ps 50:14 [Vulgate version: et spiritu potenti confirma me].

62 SAINT TERESA OF JESUS, Way of Perfection, 335, 2.

63 PC 5; RD 7.

213

44. We want to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible. He teaches us, I have given you an example (Jn 13:15). Saint Paul exhorts, Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus (Phil 2:5). We must be the aroma of Christ (2 Cor 2:15), ambassadors for Christ (2 Cor 5:20)... of the mystery of the Gospel (Eph 6:19), [the] letter of Christ (2 Cor 3:3), [we must] put on Christ (Gal 3:27).We must be firmly convinced that we are predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29), reproducing Him,65 becoming similar to Him,66 configuring ourselves to Him,67 and knowing that we reflect the same image (2 Cor 3:18) of the only Son of God. We want to imitate Him until we can truly say to others, Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Cor 11:1); and, It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20).

45. The Word assumed human nature. This should move us to practice the virtues of self-denial: humility, poverty, suffering, obedience, self-surrender, mercy and charity to all men.

46. Since the Word became man without ceasing to be God, we must learn how to be in the world68 “without being of the world.”69 We must go into the world in order to convert it and not to imitate it; to enter cultures not to convert ourselves into these cultures, but to heal them and to elevate them with the strength of the Gospel, doing as Christ did: “The Son took away the devil’s nature, assumed human nature, and conferred the divine nature.”70

64 Cf. LG 44.

65 Cf. Rom 8:29.

66 Cf. Phil 3:10.

67 Cf. Phil 3:21.

68 Cf. Jn 17:11.

69 Cf. Jn 17:14-16.

70 BLESSED ISAAC DE STELLA, Sermon 11. ML 194, 1728.

214

47. Christ became like us yet without sin (Heb 4:15). Therefore, sin, error, and all its derivatives are not assumable. Before baptizing, exorcism is necessary; without conversion, reconciliation is impossible and without renouncing evil, redemption does not exist. Unity cannot exist at the cost of truth. There is no holiness without cleansing the soul: “Holiness means cleansing.”71

48. Only things that have dignity or are necessary can be assumed. Inhuman, antihuman, or infrahuman things cannot be assumed. Likewise, irrational or absurd things, or anything derived from them, cannot be assumed.

49. Since Christ assumed a complete human nature, nothing genuinely human can be rejected. We must assume all that is human because “anything that wasn’t taken, was not redeemed,”72 and anything human that is not assumed “becomes a new idol replete with all the old malicious cunning.”73

50. Assuming what is human must not only be apparent, but real. The only real assumption is the one that truly transforms what is human into Christ, [thus] elevating it, dignifying it and perfecting it. What is left merely at the human level has only seemingly been assumed.

71 SAINT JOHN OF AVILA, Treatise about the Priesthood, 12.

72 SAINT GREGORY OF NACIANZUS, Epistles, 101; MG 37,181; AG 3, footnote
